title: The Imperfect --- the Past That Kept Going

lessons.title: hablaba — let a past action stay open
lessons.gloss: the singular -ar imperfect — hablaba, hablabas, hablaba

segments.text: Hablé español presents speaking as a completed past event. A different past, the imperfect, can leave the action open: Hablaba español — “I was speaking Spanish” or “I used to speak Spanish.” The sentence does not say where the action ended.

utterances: person: yo. open or habitual past: hablaba.
person: tú. open or habitual past: hablabas.
person: él / ella / usted. open or habitual past: hablaba.

segments.text: Say hablaba, hablabas, hablaba. The first and third forms are identical; the surrounding conversation or an explicit person tells you who is speaking. Plural persons wait.
Spanish -aba continues the Latin imperfect family in -ābam. Historical sound change reshaped the complete Latin forms, but the b remains a useful audible bridge between -ābam and Spanish -aba.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular imperfect forms of hablar: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Keep habl- and retrieve -aba, -abas, -aba.

segments.prompt: Which form leaves 'I spoke' open or habitual: hablé or hablaba?

feedback.correct: Right: hablaba leaves the past action open or habitual.
feedback.incorrect: Hablé presents a completed event; hablaba leaves it open or habitual.

segments.prompt: Which consonant links Latin -ābam with Spanish -aba?

feedback.correct: Right: the b remains audible in Spanish -aba.
feedback.incorrect: Listen inside both endings: -ābam and -aba contain b.

segments.text: Give the three learned forms. (Hablaba, hablabas, hablaba.) What can the imperfect do? (Leave a past action ongoing or habitual.) Which Latin family stands behind -aba? (-ābam.) Next: build the same gentle frame with comer.

lessons.title: comía — hear both vowels
lessons.gloss: the singular -er imperfect — comía, comías, comía

segments.text: Comí presents eating as completed. Comía leaves it open or habitual: “I was eating” or “I used to eat.” One accent separates the two forms in writing and in sound.

utterances: person: yo. open or habitual past: comía.
person: tú. open or habitual past: comías.
person: él / ella / usted. open or habitual past: comía.

segments.text: Say comía, comías, comía. As with hablaba, the first and third forms match. Plural persons wait.
The accent in -ía keeps i and a in separate syllables: co-mí-a, three beats. It appears in every form learned here. Compare final stress in comí with the middle stress and extra syllable in comía.

The -er imperfect continues a Romance reshaping of Latin -ēbam material. Among the changes, an intervocalic b was lost; later Spanish spelling marks the stressed í that keeps i-a apart. This is a layered history, not a single instruction to delete one letter.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular imperfect forms of comer: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Keep com- and retrieve -ía, -ías, -ía.

segments.prompt: Which form means 'I was eating': comí or comía?

feedback.correct: Right: comía leaves the eating in progress.
feedback.incorrect: Comí is completed; comía is ongoing or habitual.

segments.prompt: Write comía with syllable breaks.

feedback.incorrect: The accented í stays separate from a: co-mí-a.

segments.text: Give the three learned forms. (Comía, comías, comía.) What does the accent do? (Keeps i and a apart.) Which Latin family lies behind the ending? (-ēbam, reshaped through Romance.) Next: test whether vivir can reuse this row.

lessons.title: vivía — reuse the complete -er row
lessons.gloss: the singular -ir imperfect — vivía, vivías, vivía

segments.text: Chapter 15 let comer and vivir share one completed-past row. They converge again here. Replace com- in comía, comías, comía with viv-.

utterances: person: yo. comer: comía. vivir: vivía.
person: tú. comer: comías. vivir: vivías.
person: él / ella / usted. comer: comía. vivir: vivía.

segments.text: Say vivía, vivías, vivía. -er and -ir share -ía, -ías, -ía. The accent still keeps i-a apart. Plural persons wait.
Viví en Madrid. — presents living there as a completed stretch.
Vivía en Madrid. — puts us inside that past stretch or treats it as background.
Both are past. The speaker chooses how to frame the event.

Vivir continues Latin vīvere. Its infinitive belongs to the Spanish -ir class, but the imperfect has converged with -er. That shared row is a reliable fact about these learned forms, not a claim that the two conjugations are identical everywhere.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: “Viví en Madrid. Vivía en Madrid.”]

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular imperfect forms of vivir: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Keep viv- and reuse -ía, -ías, -ía.

segments.prompt: Which two infinitive classes share the learned imperfect endings -ía, -ías, -ía?

feedback.correct: Right: -er and -ir share this imperfect row.
feedback.incorrect: Compare comer and vivir: -er and -ir share the row.

segments.prompt: Say 'I was living in Madrid' in Spanish.

feedback.incorrect: Use imperfect vivía, then known en Madrid.

segments.text: Give the three vivir forms. (Vivía, vivías, vivía.) Which class shares them? (-er.) What contrast can viví / vivía make? (Completed stretch versus an open or background past.) Next: learn ver before asking it to enter this tense.

lessons.title: ver — learn the verb before its past

segments.text: Ver means “to see.” Its written v uses the Spanish sound you already know: it is not contrasted with a separate English-style v sound. Say ver.

utterances: person: yo. present: veo.
person: tú. present: ves.
person: él / ella / usted. present: ve.

segments.text: The tú and third-person forms resemble the familiar -er row. The yo form keeps an extra vowel: veo. Reuse known café: Veo café — “I see coffee.”

Spanish ver continues Latin vidēre, “to see,” through Old Spanish veer. Loss of the consonant between vowels helps explain the shorter shape; the two adjacent vowels later contracted in the infinitive. English video belongs to the same Latin family, a memory bridge rather than a new Spanish word for this lesson.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: “ver comes through veer from vidēre”]

segments.prompt: What does Spanish ver mean?

feedback.incorrect: Ver is the infinitive 'to see'.

segments.prompt: Give the learned present forms of ver: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Retrieve the short row: veo, ves, ve.

segments.prompt: Which Latin verb stands behind Spanish ver: vidēre or īre?

feedback.incorrect: Choose the sight verb vidēre; īre is the source of ir.

segments.text: What does ver mean? (“To see.”) Give its three learned present forms. (Veo, ves, ve.) Which Latin verb stands behind it? (Vidēre.) Next: add ser to the open past.

lessons.title: era — an old root in an open past
lessons.gloss: the singular imperfect of ser — era, eras, era

segments.text: You know present soy, eres, es and completed-past fui, fuiste, fue. The open or background past of ser uses a different short stem: era.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the singular ser row

utterances: person: yo. open or background past: era.
person: tú. open or background past: eras.
person: él / ella / usted. open or background past: era.

segments.text: Say era, eras, era. The first and third forms match, just as they did in the regular imperfect rows. ¿Era usted? asks “Was it you?” without adding a new noun. Plural persons wait.

Era continues Latin eram, an old form in the esse family. That is the family already connected to Spanish ser and English essence. The preterite fue comes from another historical set, so era / fue is a real contrast inside one modern verb.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular imperfect forms of ser: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Retrieve the short row era, eras, era.

segments.prompt: Which ser form presents a background past: era or fue?

feedback.correct: Right: era supplies the background or open past.
feedback.incorrect: Fue presents a bounded event; era supplies background.

segments.prompt: Which Latin form stands directly behind Spanish era: eram or ībam?

feedback.correct: Right: Spanish era continues Latin eram.
feedback.incorrect: Eram belongs to the esse family; ībam stands behind iba.

segments.text: Give the three learned ser forms. (Era, eras, era.) Which past form supplies background, era or fue? (Era.) Which Latin form stands behind it? (Eram.) Next: follow ir back toward its own older verb.

lessons.title: iba — ir returns to its inherited past
lessons.gloss: the singular imperfect of ir — iba, ibas, iba

segments.text: Present voy and completed-past fui came from different historical sets. For an open or habitual past, ir gives you iba — “I was going” or “I used to go.”

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the singular ir row

utterances: person: yo. open or habitual past: iba.
person: tú. open or habitual past: ibas.
person: él / ella / usted. open or habitual past: iba.

segments.text: Say iba, ibas, iba. Reuse the destination frame: Iba a Madrid — “I was going to Madrid” or “I used to go to Madrid.” Plural persons wait.

Iba continues Latin ībam, from īre, the inherited verb behind the Spanish infinitive ir. Present voy contains material associated with vādere, while preterite fui comes from the Latin “be” perfect family. These sources help explain the three learned sets; they do not mean that every form in every tense can be assigned to one source by a three-box rule.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: “Fui a Madrid. Iba a Madrid.”]

feedback.incorrect: Retrieve the short row iba, ibas, iba.

segments.prompt: Say 'I was going to Madrid' in Spanish.

feedback.incorrect: Use imperfect iba, then known a Madrid.

segments.prompt: Which inherited Latin verb stands behind iba: īre or vidēre?

feedback.correct: Right: iba continues ībam from īre.
feedback.incorrect: Choose the motion verb īre; vidēre means 'see'.

segments.text: Give the three learned forms. (Iba, ibas, iba.) Say “I was going to Madrid.” (Iba a Madrid.) Which Latin form stands behind iba? (Ībam, from īre.) Next: put newly learned ver into the same past.

lessons.title: veía — keep the extra e you already met
lessons.gloss: the singular imperfect of ver — veía, veías, veía

segments.text: You learned ver before its past: veo, ves, ve. Its imperfect keeps ve- and adds the familiar -ía row. That gives veía — “I was seeing” or “I used to see.”

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the singular ver row

utterances: person: yo. open or habitual past: veía.
person: tú. open or habitual past: veías.
person: él / ella / usted. open or habitual past: veía.

segments.text: Say veía, veías, veía. Keep í-a in separate syllables. Plural persons wait.

Old Spanish veer displays the ve- shape clearly. The imperfect veía preserves that vowel before the familiar -ía material. It is useful to call this an exceptional learned row, but not to pretend that ver was already known before this chapter or that the history is merely “regular plus one letter.”

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular imperfect forms of ver: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Keep ve- and retrieve -ía, -ías, -ía.

segments.prompt: Which sentence means 'I was seeing coffee': Veo café or Veía café?

feedback.correct: Right: Veía café uses the open past.
feedback.incorrect: Veo is present; veía is the imperfect.

segments.prompt: Which earlier Spanish form makes the extra e of veía easier to see: veer or ir?

feedback.correct: Right: Old Spanish veer displays the ve- shape.
feedback.incorrect: Choose veer, the earlier form in the vidēre family.

segments.text: Give the three learned forms. (Veía, veías, veía.) Which vowel stays before -ía? (e.) Which earlier form displays it? (Veer.) Next: retrieve every Chapter 16 row and make a few bounded contrasts.

lessons.title: Practice — keep the past open or close it
lessons.gloss: a singular checkpoint for the open past and the completed-past contrast

segments.text: This checkpoint adds no vocabulary and no plural persons. Retrieve the seven learned singular rows, then choose whether a known sentence presents the past as completed or leaves it open as background, progress, or habit.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the complete Chapter 16 frame

segments.text: Regular rows:
yo: hablaba, comía, vivía.
tú: hablabas, comías, vivías.
él / ella / usted: hablaba, comía, vivía.
The three special rows:
yo: era, iba, veía.
tú: eras, ibas, veías.
él / ella / usted: era, iba, veía.
The first and third forms match in every learned row. Comer and vivir share -ía, -ías, -ía. Ver keeps ve- before that material. Plural persons remain outside this checkpoint.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one scene, two frames

segments.text: Hablé español. — completed event. Hablaba español. — open, background, or habitual speaking.
Viví en Madrid. — completed stretch. Vivía en Madrid. — we stand inside that past stretch.
Fui a Madrid. — completed trip. Iba a Madrid. — motion was in progress or habitual.
The tense does not mechanically report how long something lasted. It frames the past from a different viewpoint.

-aba continues the Latin -ābam family. -ía continues material from the -ēbam family after several Romance changes. Era continues eram; iba continues ībam from īre; and veía keeps the ve- shape also visible in Old Spanish veer. These are historical bridges, not recipes for generating unlearned forms.

segments.text: Give the six yo forms. (Hablaba, comía, vivía, era, iba, veía.) Which two regular classes share a row? (-er and -ir.) What is the core contrast? (The preterite presents a completed event; the imperfect leaves past action open, habitual, in progress, or in the background.) Chapter 17 can now build on -ía without borrowing a plural form here.
